Cross Circle

GeometryCirclesTriangles
Game: A triangle, a point and a circle cross its sides again and again; watch where the new lines meet when you move the points.
How to play: Drag A, B, C or P with a mouse or finger, or focus a point and use the arrow keys. Press Hint to reveal the circle's centre, Move P for a new place, or Reset to start over.
Look for the math

Drop three perpendiculars from P onto the sides of a triangle. Their feet lie on a circle, and that circle cuts each side again. The three lines drawn at those new crossings always arrive at the same place, and that place has a simple description. The live cut-the-knot page still embeds Bogomolny's Java applet (it asks for an old Java VM); this page draws the same construction with draggable points.

The circle through the feet

The three feet are the corners of the pedal triangle of P. Three points fix a circle unless they are in a straight line. When P happens to lie on the circumcircle of ABC, its feet do line up — the Simson line — so the original page carefully says the circle crosses the sides again in general. Press Move P or drag it away from that circle and the pedal circle returns.

Why the three lines meet

Let O be the centre of the pedal circle and let N be the foot of the perpendicular from O onto one side line. A chord's midpoint is the projection of its circle's centre, so N is halfway between the two crossings on that side. The other crossing is 2N − first foot. Now take S, the half-turn image of P in O: S = 2O − P. Projection onto a straight line shares addition and scaling, so the projection of S on the side is 2N − first foot as well. Therefore the perpendicular at the second crossing goes through S. The same argument works on all three sides, so the three lines concur at S. Press Hint to see O and the three chord midpoints.

What the checks found

The logic test compares this page with a second transcription of the applet's own drawing methods on 72 starting positions plus more than 1,400 random triangles with P anywhere in the board. On every non-degenerate picture, both crossings lie on the circle and all three perpendiculars pass through S to better than a billionth of the circle's radius, so the page's "always concur" claim holds. Two faithful quirks survive: the applet takes its radius as the average of the three distances from the centre, and its foot routine snaps P to itself when P comes within sqrt(0.1) of a side's endpoint; in that tiny zone the drawn crossing shifts a little. When the feet are collinear the test checks that no circle is drawn, as the page's "in general" allows.

Try dragging P nearly onto the triangle's circumcircle: the circle grows huge and S runs far away. Press Hint to watch O and the chord midpoints follow it.
